note: Read: page 4, of Glessner House at 1800 South Prairie Avenue, 'The house is modified Romanesque in style, characterized by rugged masonry, a round arch motif, striking window-wall relationships, and a simple geometric form defined by the relationship of walls to the red-tiled, gabled roof.' Page 18: 'The John J. Glessner House is Henry Hobson Richardson's magnificent tribute to the Romanesque. The William W. Kimball House, patterned after the Chateau de Josselin in France, illustrates nineteenth century America's imitative attempt at duplicating the classical opulence of Europe. The Joseph G. Coleman House is an elegant amalgamation of the styles found in both the Glessner and Kimball mansions.' Page 19: 'Two stories high, with both a full basement and attic, the house is faced with heavily rusticated Wellesley granite.' And: 'With Richardson's work came the first break with traditional, classic forms of design and detail. And because that happened, a whole new style of American architecture was allowed to grow to maturity in the work of the "Chicago School". Flourishing in the 1880s and '90s, the Chicago School was a specific style of commercial architecture typified by the introduction of the structural steel frame and embracing design principles totally without reference to historical styles.' Then: 'Glessner House was not only one of Richardson's greatest achievements, but it was also a model, along with his Marshall Field Wholesale Store, [which would] later influence such famous architects as John Root, Louis Sullivan, and Frank Lloyd Wright.' Page 17: prepared by John F. Hern, Commission on Chicago Historical and Architectural Landmarks, 3/17/72; the State Liaison Officer's nomination dated April 5, 1972.
